description: Deterministic approval-readiness policy for ei-scope-validator. It answers a different question from ei-scope-resolver's scope-policy.json: not 'is this artifact internally consistent?' but 'is this scope narrow and defensible enough to put in front of a human, and did a writing stage stay inside it?'. Rules only ever record findings; they never widen a scope or downgrade a resolver finding.

reuses.note: Hard size limits and the scope-level confidence floor are owned by the resolver policy and are not restated here.

rules.message: The proposed scope is not 'resolved', so there is nothing defensible to approve. Answer the resolver findings and re-run the resolver.
The proposed files span more implementation areas than a single story should touch. Split the story or justify the spread and re-resolve.
A proposed file is below the per-file confidence floor, so it is a guess rather than a conclusion. Strengthen the evidence or drop the file.
A file is proposed for modification without naming a symbol, so its blast radius is the whole file. Name the symbols that change.
A proposed file has no related test that names it, so the change would be unprovable. Identify the test, or state why none can exist.
A high-severity risk is recorded against this scope. A human must answer it before approval, not during implementation.
The proposed scope is larger than a routine change, so the approver should confirm the breadth is intended.
The proposed scope creates several new files, which widens the surface the approver is authorising.
The proposed scope deletes files. Deletions are irreversible for the approver, so they are surfaced explicitly.
The scope records an unresolved dependency. It is not in scope and must not be absorbed during implementation.
A file was changed that the sealed scope does not authorise. Raise a scope-change request; do not widen the seal.
A file inside a declared protected area was changed. This is never resolved by widening the scope.
